spark.summary: Rate limiting enforces caps on request or resource consumption per caller, tenant, or endpoint over time to protect downstream capacity, ensure fair multi-tenant sharing, and blunt abuse.
spark.keyTakeaway: Pair an in-memory local limiter (token bucket) for sub-millisecond burst protection with a Redis Lua sliding-window or token-bucket store for global tenant quotas, and always return HTTP 429 with `Retry-After`.

concept.whyItMatters: Without rate limiting, a single buggy client retry loop, scraper, or noisy tenant can saturate database connection pools and cause cascading 503 outages for every customer. Well-tuned limiters shed excess load at the edge in <1 ms while preserving headroom for healthy traffic.
whenToUse: Protecting public APIs, login/OTP endpoints, and expensive compute routes (LLM inference, PDF export) from abuse, scraping, and brute-force attacks.
Enforcing tiered SaaS commercial quotas (e.g., Free: 60 req/min, Pro: 1,000 req/min) and preventing noisy-neighbor starvation in multi-tenant platforms.
Shielding downstream databases or third-party webhooks with fixed concurrency or RPS ceilings.
whenNotToUse: Internal health-check, readiness, and Prometheus metrics scrape paths—throttling these triggers false-positive pod restarts.
When the bottleneck is purely slow downstream processing rather than request rate; use adaptive concurrency limits (e.g., Vegas/Gradient2) or backpressure instead.
Strictly idempotent, cache-absorbed static CDN assets where edge PoPs already absorb 99%+ of traffic cheaply.
keyPoints: Token Bucket allows controlled bursts up to bucket capacity `B` while capping sustained average rate at `R` tokens/sec—ideal for interactive APIs.
Leaky Bucket (queue-based) smooths bursty ingress into a constant egress rate, protecting brittle downstream sinks at the cost of queueing latency.
Fixed Window Counters suffer from 2x boundary-burst spikes at minute/hour rollovers; Sliding Window Counters eliminate boundary spikes with O(1) memory.
Distributed rate limiting requires atomic read-modify-write (Redis Lua scripts or Envoy `ratelimit` gRPC) to prevent race conditions across gateway replicas.
Standardize responses with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests`, `Retry-After`, and IETF `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining`, and `RateLimit-Reset` headers.

examples.title: Stripe-Style Dual-Layer Token Bucket & Concurrency Limiter
examples.scenario: A payment API serves 100 req/s per merchant in live mode, but bursts of webhook-triggered queries occasionally spike to 250 req/s for 2 seconds.
examples.outcome: A Redis-backed Token Bucket (refill=100/s, capacity=200) absorbs short legitimate bursts, while a separate concurrency semaphore caps slow `/v1/reports` queries at 10 in-flight per merchant.

examples.title: Envoy Global Rate Limit + Local Failover
examples.scenario: An API gateway cluster of 40 Envoy pods enforces a 5,000 req/hr quota per API key via a central Redis-backed `ratelimit` gRPC service.
examples.outcome: When a Redis shard experiences a 400 ms failover, Envoy's `failure_mode_deny: false` (fail-open) + local per-pod 200 req/s circuit-breaker cap prevents a total outage while still blocking runaway floods.

tradeOffs.pro: Synchronous Redis Lua checks enforce exact cross-region or cross-pod quotas.
tradeOffs.con: Adds 0.5-2 ms network RTT per request and makes Redis availability a critical-path dependency.

tradeOffs.pro: Fail-open preserves user traffic if the rate-limit store goes down.
tradeOffs.con: Leaves origin servers exposed to overload during a limiter outage unless backed by a local fallback limiter.

tradeOffs.factor: Sliding Window Log vs. Sliding Window Counter
tradeOffs.pro: Sliding Window Log (Redis `ZSET` of timestamps) is 100% exact to the millisecond.
tradeOffs.con: Stores O(N) timestamps per key, blowing up RAM for high-rate tenants; Sliding Window Counter approximates it in O(1) space.

failureModes.name: Hot-Key Contention in Redis
failureModes.description: A single global or mega-tenant key (e.g., `rl:global` or a major customer) routes 100k RPS to one Redis shard, saturating its single-threaded event loop.
failureModes.mitigation: Batch token leases locally at the gateway (e.g., fetch 50 tokens at a time) or shard the key across N slots (`key:{0..15}`) with N-way split quotas.

failureModes.name: Fixed-Window Boundary Stampede
failureModes.description: A client sends 1,000 requests at 12:00:59 and another 1,000 at 12:01:01, hitting 2x the intended 1,000 req/min limit in 2 seconds.
failureModes.mitigation: Replace fixed windows with Sliding Window Counter (weighted interpolation of current and previous bucket) or Token Bucket.

failureModes.name: Retry Storm Amplification
failureModes.description: Blocked clients immediately retry 429 responses in a tight loop, multiplying ingress load on the rate limiter itself.
failureModes.mitigation: Return explicit `Retry-After` headers, reject early at the L7 edge/WAF before auth/DB work, and require exponential backoff + jitter in SDKs.

failureModes.name: Proxy IP Spoofing / Shared NAT Collisions
failureModes.description: Keying strictly on `X-Forwarded-For` allows header spoofing, while keying on raw IP throttles an entire corporate NAT or mobile carrier.
failureModes.mitigation: Parse only trusted proxy hops for client IP, and key authenticated endpoints on `tenant_id` or `api_key_hash` rather than IP alone.

commonMistakes: Using separate `GET` then `INCR` commands in Redis without a Lua script, creating race conditions under concurrent requests.
Leaving Redis keys without `EXPIRE` / `PEXPIRE` TTLs, causing unbounded memory growth from one-off caller IPs.
Rate limiting after expensive JWT signature verification, body parsing, or DB lookups instead of at the outermost edge.
Applying identical limits to `GET /health`, `POST /login`, and `POST /export` instead of endpoint-tiered cost weights.
Returning `500` or `503` instead of `429 Too Many Requests`, confusing client SDKs into aggressive immediate retries.

sections.content:
## The idea

Rate limiting decouples **incoming demand** from **system capacity** by enforcing a strict admission budget over time. Every request is classified by a rate-limit key—such as `ip`, `api_key`, `tenant_id:route`, or `user_id`—and checked against a stateful quota before expensive business logic executes.

Production limiters balance three competing goals: **burst tolerance** (letting legitimate users load a dashboard with 15 parallel API calls), **steady-state smoothing** (keeping average RPS within DB/CPU budgets), and **low-overhead enforcement** (deciding allow/deny in $< 1\text{ ms}$ without becoming the bottleneck).

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an API gateway enforcing a **100 req/s sustained, 200-request burst** Token Bucket per API key using an atomic Redis Lua script (`EVALSHA`):

1. **Request arrives** at Envoy/NGINX with `Authorization: Bearer sk_live_...`. The gateway extracts `key = rl:sk_live_98a` and current timestamp `now_ms`.
2. **Atomic Lua execution**: Redis runs the script single-threaded:
   - Fetches `tokens` and `last_refill_ms` from the hash `rl:sk_live_98a` (initializing to `tokens = 200` if missing).
   - Computes `elapsed = max(0, now_ms - last_refill_ms)` and `refilled = min(200, tokens + elapsed * 0.1)` (100 tokens/1000 ms).
   - If `refilled >= 1`, sets `tokens = refilled - 1`, updates `last_refill_ms = now_ms`, sets `PEXPIRE` to 10s, and returns `{1, floor(tokens), 0}`.
   - Otherwise returns `{0, 0, ceil((1 - refilled) / 0.1)}` (milliseconds until 1 token is available).
3. **Gateway response**: On `1`, the request forwards upstream with `RateLimit-Remaining`. On `0`, the gateway immediately returns `HTTP 429` with `Retry-After: 1`.

sections.content:
## Local, centralized, and hybrid architectures

- **Local in-memory limiting**: Zero network overhead (~50 ns), but each of $K$ gateway pods tracks only $1/K$ of the quota. Uneven load balancing causes premature 429s or under-enforcement.
- **Centralized Redis/Valkey**: Exact global counts across all pods, but every request pays a network hop and Redis becomes a hot-spot risk.
- **Hybrid token leasing (best of both)**: Gateways keep a local token bucket and periodically lease batches (e.g., 50 tokens or 100 ms of quota) from Redis asynchronously. This cuts Redis QPS by 50x while keeping global drift bounded to one lease window.

## Rate limiting algorithms compared

| Algorithm | Memory per Key | Burst Handling | Boundary Spike | Best Fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Token Bucket | O(1) (2 numbers) | Up to capacity `B` | None | General public APIs (Stripe, GitHub) |
| Leaky Bucket (Queue) | O(queue size) | Smooths to fixed rate | None | Protecting legacy/brittle downstream sinks |
| Fixed Window Counter | O(1) (1 integer) | Up to limit per window | **2x spike** at edges | Coarse abuse blocks where 2x spike is tolerable |
| Sliding Window Log | O(N) timestamps | Exact over rolling window | None | Low-rate strict limits (e.g., 5 OTPs / 15 min) |
| Sliding Window Counter | O(1) (2 integers) | Weighted interpolation | Negligible (<1%) | High-scale distributed APIs needing low RAM |

## Failure modes

- **Hot-key Redis saturation**: Millions of requests hitting one shared key (e.g., unauthenticated `/public` endpoint) bottleneck a single Redis core.
- **Distributed clock skew**: Using client/gateway wall-clock timestamps inside Redis Lua scripts causes negative elapsed times if one gateway's NTP drifts; always use `redis.call('TIME')` inside Lua.
- **Retry storms**: Returning `429` without `Retry-After` or jitter guidance causes aggressive clients to hammer the gateway even harder.
- **Fail-closed cascading outage**: Blocking all traffic when Redis times out turns a cache blip into a full platform outage.

## Production patterns & observability

- **Weighted cost budgets**: Charge `cost = 1` for `GET /items/{id}` and `cost = 25` for `POST /search/export` against the same tenant token bucket so heavy endpoints cannot starve cheap ones.
- **Shadow / dry-run mode**: Deploy new limits with `enforce: false` for 7 days, emitting `ratelimit_would_deny_total` metrics to spot legitimate enterprise bursts before enforcing.
- **Standardized headers**: Emit `RateLimit-Policy`, `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining`, and `RateLimit-Reset` on both `200` and `429` responses so well-behaved SDKs self-throttle proactively.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Choose Token Bucket or Sliding Window Counter for O(1) memory without 2x fixed-window boundary spikes.
- [ ] Execute distributed checks atomically (Redis Lua with `TIME` and `PEXPIRE` TTLs) to prevent race conditions and memory leaks.
- [ ] Configure a fail-open policy paired with a local per-pod safety-net limiter.
- [ ] Exempt `/healthz`, `/readyz`, and internal control-plane heartbeats from tenant rate limits.
- [ ] Return HTTP `429` with `Retry-After` and `RateLimit-*` headers, and validate limits in shadow mode first.

questions.prompt: Why are standard Redis GET and SET operations unsafe for implementing API rate limiting across multi-threaded gateway nodes?

options.text: Redis GET and SET require disk I/O flushes that stall execution.
options.explanation: Redis is in-memory and does not flush disk on standard GET/SET.

options.text: Concurrent GET and SET calls create a race condition where multiple requests read identical counter values before incrementing, over-admitting client traffic.
options.explanation: Correct! Non-atomic read-modify-write operations allow clients to bypass rate limits.

interviewProblems.title: Global Multi-Region API Rate Limiter
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are building an API Gateway for a global cloud provider serving 500,000 requests/sec across 3 geographical regions (US, EU, AP). How do you enforce a strict per-user quota of 1,000 req/min with sub-millisecond overhead?

dimensions.name: Local vs Global Counter Sync
dimensions.description: Decoupling per-region local token buckets from global asynchronous reconciliation.

dimensions.name: Atomic Edge Execution
dimensions.description: Using Redis Lua scripts at edge PoPs.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Deploy local Redis token buckets at each edge region using atomic Lua scripts. Synchronize token usage asynchronously to a global coordinator in batches to avoid cross-region latency on every request.
commonPitfalls: Making synchronous cross-region database calls on every API request.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Rate limiting enforces caps on request or resource consumption per caller, tenant, or endpoint over time to protect downstream capacity, ensure fair multi-tenant sharing, and blunt abuse.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Redis Cluster applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Upstream Service.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Upstream Service experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Batch token leases locally at the gateway (e.g., fetch 50 tokens at a time) or shard the key across N slots (`key:{0..15}`) with N-way split quotas.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Pair an in-memory local limiter (token bucket) for sub-millisecond burst protection with a Redis Lua sliding-window or token-bucket store for global tenant quotas, and always return HTTP 429 with `Retry-After`.
Avoid trap: Using separate `GET` then `INCR` commands in Redis without a Lua script, creating race conditions under concurrent requests.
Avoid trap: Leaving Redis keys without `EXPIRE` / `PEXPIRE` TTLs, causing unbounded memory growth from one-off caller IPs.
When to reach for it: Protecting public APIs, login/OTP endpoints, and expensive compute routes (LLM inference, PDF export) from abuse, scraping, and brute-force attacks.
When to reach for it: Enforcing tiered SaaS commercial quotas (e.g., Free: 60 req/min, Pro: 1,000 req/min) and preventing noisy-neighbor starvation in multi-tenant platforms.

putItTogether.title: Putting Rate Limiting Together
putItTogether.summary: Pair an in-memory local limiter (token bucket) for sub-millisecond burst protection with a Redis Lua sliding-window or token-bucket store for global tenant quotas, and always return HTTP 429 with `Retry-After`.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Rate Limiting before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: A Redis-backed Token Bucket (refill=100/s, capacity=200) absorbs short legitimate bursts, while a separate concurrency semaphore caps slow `/v1/reports` queries at 10 in-flight per merchant.
